compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
A week before the holiday season, both are called in to decide the same main display. Either person might go onto the shop floor to see what customers are doing or adjust the display when new information comes in. Those possibilities illustrate the shared E, S and P without making customer service behaviour a test of type.

Only the judging letter separates them. T more often asks whether this standard can be applied consistently to every comparable case; F more often asks what this means for specific people and whether what was promised still counts. Both look at footfall, both watch margin, and both will bend once for a regular — the difference is not whether they look, but which kind of reason they more often use to rule one of two acceptable options out.

### Adjusting the seasonal display: which basis each may weigh

In a fictional shop preparing for a holiday promotion, two display plans meet the same aisle-clearance requirements and have the same materials budget. Both people have access to last year’s foot traffic and margins.

Option A stacks every gift box by price band from top to bottom, a simple rule that staff cannot get wrong. Option B returns the boxes to the old spot by the second-floor lift entrance — the route a group of regulars walks straight past every year at this season.

The reason supporting A is more often: this banding rule applies to every category, and once it is broken for one item, every future promotion needs the exception explained again. The reason supporting B is more often: these customers asked last year whether it would be back in that spot, a promise should be kept, and if they cannot find it they will ask staff another round of questions.

Either reason can come from either person. An ESTP who has done displays for years will bring people into the judgement with "the lighting on that row is unfriendly to older customers"; an ESFP carrying a sales target will put the standard first with "this rule cannot be broken for a single item". Experience, duty and the season's goal all rewrite the choice.

The place to look is not who speaks first but where the reason lands: one asks whether the standard can be applied consistently, the other asks what it means for these specific people. Both usually appear in the same discussion; writing them down is to see which one you more often supply, not to label anyone.

### Why the auxiliary and third functions differ

The two writings are not the same two functions swapped in place. In the common four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni: both have Se dominant and Ni fourth, and the auxiliary and third positions are Fi against Ti and Te against Fe.

On the type dynamics writing used here, both lead with Se. Reaction speed, willingness to act at once and the ability to sit still for long are affected by many factors and cannot separate ESFP from ESTP. What can be compared is the auxiliary: Fi weighs a choice against personally held values. Ti examines whether the reasoning behind a choice is internally consistent. Either person can also account for the effects on customers and check the store’s criteria. The third position, Te and Fe, is often written as a preference in organising and expressing outward — one more often pushing by checkable results and process, the other by shared atmosphere and how those present feel. Whether that position carries an attitude label is not consistent across sources, some tables giving only the function name; this page marks the common writing and does not present it as the only version.

Ni in fourth place is only a position in the model, not a defect, and it does not explain someone’s ability to plan ahead. A position describes emphasis in the model, and predicts neither behavioural order, a field of expertise, nor how well two people work together or who attracts whom. Base descriptions are in the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
The three scenes below are editorial fictions about a store and a drive, used only to see which reasons each may cite in front of the same information. The division of work and the outcome are decided by experience, duty, staffing and checkable data, not by type.

### Display day: who gets the main table

(Fictional scene.) Three days before the mid-autumn festival, the store has one main display table, three side shelves, the same three staff, one margin sheet and one sales forecast.

Two directions are both viable: make the main table into a scene people want to photograph, or stack the two highest-margin gift boxes on it. The reason for the first is more often: families with children will stop for a photo, and the store's reputation in this area rests on that; the reason for the second is more often: the main table goes to the top two by margin, the rule was used last season, and changing it now needs an explanation.

Both are counting the same thing — the margin on those two boxes, the forecast, how much side-shelf space is left. The difference is which reason is put first, not who ignores the data.

The result can only be judged by results: compare sales, margin, shrinkage and footfall counts after the same season. An option that sells more may be selling because of the position, or because those two boxes were scarce anyway; attributing the outcome to a type has no basis. A common compromise on the floor is to keep a photo spot on the main table and give the two metres by the side shelf and the till to add-on items — that is a division of tasks, unrelated to which type anyone is.

The check belongs in the layout review: on display day, photograph the overall layout, the view down the main aisle and the space near the checkout from repeatable viewpoints. To examine where people stop, record observations by location in the same time windows. The photos are for reviewing the layout and the counts for checking the judgement; neither is for inferring a type.

### Cutting the price on short-dated stock

(Fictional scene.) A batch of yoghurt has four days of shelf life left. Both have the same batch, the same discount authority (30% off at most), the same margin floor, and the same two days to clear it.

One direction gathers it onto a small table and puts the date and the discount on one sign; the other keeps it in place and uses the same markdown rule across the relevant shelf locations. The reason for the first is more often: let people see it clearly before they take it, rather than discover the date at home; the reason for the second is more often: treat one batch of short-dated stock by one rule, and do not give an extra step of discount because a particular item sells well.

Either direction can clear it, and either can leave remnants. Discounting too deep damages margin, unclear labelling damages trust; both costs have nothing to do with type and everything to do with discount authority, shelf position and the footfall of those days. Results are checked with sales, margin, shrinkage and complaint records, not used to infer anyone's type.

Date labelling and discount execution follow store policy and local regulation. This section covers only how the two state their reasons; it does not say what discount to set, nor whether short-dated stock should be sold at all.

### A weekend drive: changing the route on the way

(Fictional scene.) A few people drive out for the weekend, traffic stops shortly after joining the motorway, and the front passenger asks whether to go somewhere else. This scene covers communication and the organisation of information only: the route and whether to divert are decided by the driver under traffic rules, navigation and the road conditions, and are not argued while driving; if it needs discussing, stop somewhere safe first, and handle any incident or breakdown under traffic police and recovery guidance.

Both hold the same information: fuel left, the detour time from navigation, where the others originally wanted to go, and the latest time to turn back. One more often puts "what does everyone want from this trip" first: who has looked forward to it for ages, whose expectation is disappointed by a change; the other more often puts "do the constraints hold for everyone equally" first: is there enough fuel and time, and do the things promised in the original plan still count.

Both reasons appear and both miss something: attending only to expectations may ignore the fuel gauge, attending only to constraints may leave the carful of people unhappy. Who answers which message first is not a criterion — who was driving and who was reading navigation decides that far more than type. Before the next trip, put both "where we most want to go" and "the latest time to turn back" into the group, and both questions get answered, which is more useful than watching who answers first.

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is giving each a label: risk-taking to ESTP, sociability to ESFP. Whether someone steps up in a sudden situation depends on experience, physical capacity, duty and how many people are present; both types can step up, and both can finish a stock count quietly.

The second is judging by spending and saving habits. Consumption style alone cannot separate T from F; a spending decision also has to be read against income, family responsibilities and the goal at the time, and those conditions usually bear more directly than preference.

The third slip is writing T as "only numbers, no humanity" and F as "only feelings, no rules". ESTP will also stand up for a colleague who has been treated badly, and ESFP can cut an unprofitable category by a rule. What can be compared is the reason: does it more often cite "can this standard be applied consistently", or "what does this mean for the people involved". Both reasons are used by both, a single phrasing is not a criterion, and it has to be read across comparable situations.

(Fictional scene.) Three days before the mid-autumn festival, the store has one main display table, three side shelves, the same three staff, one margin sheet and one sales forecast.

Two directions are both viable: make the main table into a scene people want to photograph, or stack the two highest-margin gift boxes on it. The reason for the first is more often: families with children will stop for a photo, and the store's reputation in this area rests on that; the reason for the second is more often: the main table goes to the top two by margin, the rule was used last season, and changing it now needs an explanation.

An option that sells more may be selling because of the position, or because those two boxes were scarce anyway; attributing the outcome to a type has no basis. sections.title: Quick answer

body: A week before the holiday season, both are called in to decide the same main display. Either person might go onto the shop floor to see what customers are doing or adjust the display when new information comes in. Those possibilities illustrate the shared E, S and P without making customer service behaviour a test of type.

Only the judging letter separates them. T more often asks whether this standard can be applied consistently to every comparable case; F more often asks what this means for specific people and whether what was promised still counts. Both look at footfall, both watch margin, and both will bend once for a regular — the difference is not whether they look, but which kind of reason they more often use to rule one of two acceptable options out.
### Adjusting the seasonal display: which basis each may weigh

In a fictional shop preparing for a holiday promotion, two display plans meet the same aisle-clearance requirements and have the same materials budget. Both people have access to last year’s foot traffic and margins.

Option A stacks every gift box by price band from top to bottom, a simple rule that staff cannot get wrong. Option B returns the boxes to the old spot by the second-floor lift entrance — the route a group of regulars walks straight past every year at this season.

The reason supporting A is more often: this banding rule applies to every category, and once it is broken for one item, every future promotion needs the exception explained again. The reason supporting B is more often: these customers asked last year whether it would be back in that spot, a promise should be kept, and if they cannot find it they will ask staff another round of questions.

Either reason can come from either person. An ESTP who has done displays for years will bring people into the judgement with "the lighting on that row is unfriendly to older customers"; an ESFP carrying a sales target will put the standard first with "this rule cannot be broken for a single item". Experience, duty and the season's goal all rewrite the choice.

The place to look is not who speaks first but where the reason lands: one asks whether the standard can be applied consistently, the other asks what it means for these specific people. Both usually appear in the same discussion; writing them down is to see which one you more often supply, not to label anyone.
### Why the auxiliary and third functions differ

The two writings are not the same two functions swapped in place. In the common four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and ESTP is Se–Ti–Fe–Ni: both have Se dominant and Ni fourth, and the auxiliary and third positions are Fi against Ti and Te against Fe.

On the type dynamics writing used here, both lead with Se. Reaction speed, willingness to act at once and the ability to sit still for long are affected by many factors and cannot separate ESFP from ESTP. What can be compared is the auxiliary: Fi weighs a choice against personally held values. Ti examines whether the reasoning behind a choice is internally consistent. Either person can also account for the effects on customers and check the store’s criteria. The third position, Te and Fe, is often written as a preference in organising and expressing outward — one more often pushing by checkable results and process, the other by shared atmosphere and how those present feel. Whether that position carries an attitude label is not consistent across sources, some tables giving only the function name; this page marks the common writing and does not present it as the only version.

Ni in fourth place is only a position in the model, not a defect, and it does not explain someone’s ability to plan ahead. A position describes emphasis in the model, and predicts neither behavioural order, a field of expertise, nor how well two people work together or who attracts whom. Base descriptions are in the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).

body: The three scenes below are editorial fictions about a store and a drive, used only to see which reasons each may cite in front of the same information. The division of work and the outcome are decided by experience, duty, staffing and checkable data, not by type.
### Display day: who gets the main table
(Fictional scene.) Three days before the mid-autumn festival, the store has one main display table, three side shelves, the same three staff, one margin sheet and one sales forecast.

Two directions are both viable: make the main table into a scene people want to photograph, or stack the two highest-margin gift boxes on it. The reason for the first is more often: families with children will stop for a photo, and the store's reputation in this area rests on that; the reason for the second is more often: the main table goes to the top two by margin, the rule was used last season, and changing it now needs an explanation.
Both are counting the same thing — the margin on those two boxes, the forecast, how much side-shelf space is left. The difference is which reason is put first, not who ignores the data.

The result can only be judged by results: compare sales, margin, shrinkage and footfall counts after the same season. An option that sells more may be selling because of the position, or because those two boxes were scarce anyway; attributing the outcome to a type has no basis. A common compromise on the floor is to keep a photo spot on the main table and give the two metres by the side shelf and the till to add-on items — that is a division of tasks, unrelated to which type anyone is.

The check belongs in the layout review: on display day, photograph the overall layout, the view down the main aisle and the space near the checkout from repeatable viewpoints. To examine where people stop, record observations by location in the same time windows. The photos are for reviewing the layout and the counts for checking the judgement; neither is for inferring a type.
### Cutting the price on short-dated stock

(Fictional scene.) A batch of yoghurt has four days of shelf life left. Both have the same batch, the same discount authority (30% off at most), the same margin floor, and the same two days to clear it.

One direction gathers it onto a small table and puts the date and the discount on one sign; the other keeps it in place and uses the same markdown rule across the relevant shelf locations. The reason for the first is more often: let people see it clearly before they take it, rather than discover the date at home; the reason for the second is more often: treat one batch of short-dated stock by one rule, and do not give an extra step of discount because a particular item sells well.

Either direction can clear it, and either can leave remnants. Discounting too deep damages margin, unclear labelling damages trust; both costs have nothing to do with type and everything to do with discount authority, shelf position and the footfall of those days. Results are checked with sales, margin, shrinkage and complaint records, not used to infer anyone's type.

Date labelling and discount execution follow store policy and local regulation. This section covers only how the two state their reasons; it does not say what discount to set, nor whether short-dated stock should be sold at all.
### A weekend drive: changing the route on the way

(Fictional scene.) A few people drive out for the weekend, traffic stops shortly after joining the motorway, and the front passenger asks whether to go somewhere else. This scene covers communication and the organisation of information only: the route and whether to divert are decided by the driver under traffic rules, navigation and the road conditions, and are not argued while driving; if it needs discussing, stop somewhere safe first, and handle any incident or breakdown under traffic police and recovery guidance.

Both hold the same information: fuel left, the detour time from navigation, where the others originally wanted to go, and the latest time to turn back. One more often puts "what does everyone want from this trip" first: who has looked forward to it for ages, whose expectation is disappointed by a change; the other more often puts "do the constraints hold for everyone equally" first: is there enough fuel and time, and do the things promised in the original plan still count.

Both reasons appear and both miss something: attending only to expectations may ignore the fuel gauge, attending only to constraints may leave the carful of people unhappy. Who answers which message first is not a criterion — who was driving and who was reading navigation decides that far more than type. Before the next trip, put both "where we most want to go" and "the latest time to turn back" into the group, and both questions get answered, which is more useful than watching who answers first.

body: The first misread is giving each a label: risk-taking to ESTP, sociability to ESFP. Whether someone steps up in a sudden situation depends on experience, physical capacity, duty and how many people are present; both types can step up, and both can finish a stock count quietly.

The second is judging by spending and saving habits. Consumption style alone cannot separate T from F; a spending decision also has to be read against income, family responsibilities and the goal at the time, and those conditions usually bear more directly than preference.

The third slip is writing T as "only numbers, no humanity" and F as "only feelings, no rules". ESTP will also stand up for a colleague who has been treated badly, and ESFP can cut an unprofitable category by a rule. What can be compared is the reason: does it more often cite "can this standard be applied consistently", or "what does this mean for the people involved". Both reasons are used by both, a single phrasing is not a criterion, and it has to be read across comparable situations.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring convention first, then the situation you answered from: a recent job change, a new colleague to train, a target just assigned — such conditions amplify one side. None of it allows a stable tendency to be inferred from one score.

Put the practice on real decisions and record three things: what options and constraints there were, what you finally based the trade-off on, and what would change your mind. Take a few recent small matters about display, scheduling or purchasing, write a few lines for each, and look back once several are filled; that is more useful than trying to recall who you resemble during a test. If "is the standard consistent" or "what does it mean for people" keeps appearing, it is worth discussing as your judging habit; it is not a typing rule. When results disagree, check the item bank, the language and the answering situation, and do not treat behaviour when alone, or some fixed number of occasions, as the arbiter.

Reaction speed, willingness to act at once and the ability to sit still for long are affected by many factors and cannot separate ESFP from ESTP. What can be compared is the auxiliary: Fi weighs a choice against personally held values. Ti examines whether the reasoning behind a choice is internally consistent. Either person can also account for the effects on customers and check the store’s criteria. The third position, Te and Fe, is often written as a preference in organising and expressing outward — one more often pushing by checkable results and process, the other by shared atmosphere and how those present feel. Whether that position carries an attitude label is not consistent across sources, some tables giving only the function name; this page marks the common writing and does not present it as the only version.

Ni in fourth place is only a position in the model, not a defect, and it does not explain someone’s ability to plan ahead. A position describes emphasis in the model, and predicts neither behavioural order, a field of expertise, nor how well two people work together or who attracts whom. Base descriptions are in the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).
sections.title: ESFP and ESTP: shared ground and the core difference

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions first: the same season, the same shelving, the same footfall and margin data, the same materials budget, the same discount authority. Both types can use both approaches; the table records only which basis is taken first more often, and neither who moves first nor who says more enters it.

| The same event (one season, one set of shelves, one data set) | ESFP: the basis more likely attended to | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Two display options that both pass acceptance | Whether regulars will fail to find the old row, and whether the promised position should be honoured | Whether the banding rule can be applied consistently to all categories, and how an exception is explained later | Basis for judgement, T/F |
| Materials only cover half the display | Which part can be cut with the least effect on people who come often | Cut by the same priority, the same for every category | Basis for judgement, T/F |
| A customer hesitates at the shelf | Weigh what matters to the customer when comparing the same two options | Apply the same comparison criteria to both options, using the information both people have | Basis for judgement, T/F |
| The featured product has to change at short notice | Weigh how the same proposed changes would affect customers who expected the old product | Apply the same display criteria to each available replacement | Basis for judgement, T/F |
| Negotiating with a supplier | Whether a supplier of many years will struggle because of this, and will still cooperate later | Whether the same terms can be offered to other suppliers, and whether the price comparison is consistent | Basis for judgement, T/F |
| A colleague proposes an easier way to set it out | Who ends up doing one more step, and whose habit is interrupted | Whether the change muddles the original acceptance criteria | Basis for judgement, T/F |
sections.title: ESFP and ESTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
The three scenes below are editorial fictions about a store and a drive, used only to see which reasons each may cite in front of the same information. The division of work and the outcome are decided by experience, duty, staffing and checkable data, not by type.

### Display day: who gets the main table

(Fictional scene.) Three days before the mid-autumn festival, the store has one main display table, three side shelves, the same three staff, one margin sheet and one sales forecast.

Two directions are both viable: make the main table into a scene people want to photograph, or stack the two highest-margin gift boxes on it. The reason for the first is more often: families with children will stop for a photo, and the store's reputation in this area rests on that; the reason for the second is more often: the main table goes to the top two by margin, the rule was used last season, and changing it now needs an explanation.

Both are counting the same thing — the margin on those two boxes, the forecast, how much side-shelf space is left. The difference is which reason is put first, not who ignores the data.

The result can only be judged by results: compare sales, margin, shrinkage and footfall counts after the same season. An option that sells more may be selling because of the position, or because those two boxes were scarce anyway; attributing the outcome to a type has no basis. A common compromise on the floor is to keep a photo spot on the main table and give the two metres by the side shelf and the till to add-on items — that is a division of tasks, unrelated to which type anyone is.

The check belongs in the layout review: on display day, photograph the overall layout, the view down the main aisle and the space near the checkout from repeatable viewpoints. To examine where people stop, record observations by location in the same time windows. The photos are for reviewing the layout and the counts for checking the judgement; neither is for inferring a type.

### Cutting the price on short-dated stock

(Fictional scene.) A batch of yoghurt has four days of shelf life left. Both have the same batch, the same discount authority (30% off at most), the same margin floor, and the same two days to clear it.

One direction gathers it onto a small table and puts the date and the discount on one sign; the other keeps it in place and uses the same markdown rule across the relevant shelf locations. The reason for the first is more often: let people see it clearly before they take it, rather than discover the date at home; the reason for the second is more often: treat one batch of short-dated stock by one rule, and do not give an extra step of discount because a particular item sells well.

Either direction can clear it, and either can leave remnants. Discounting too deep damages margin, unclear labelling damages trust; both costs have nothing to do with type and everything to do with discount authority, shelf position and the footfall of those days. Results are checked with sales, margin, shrinkage and complaint records, not used to infer anyone's type.

Date labelling and discount execution follow store policy and local regulation. This section covers only how the two state their reasons; it does not say what discount to set, nor whether short-dated stock should be sold at all.

### A weekend drive: changing the route on the way

(Fictional scene.) A few people drive out for the weekend, traffic stops shortly after joining the motorway, and the front passenger asks whether to go somewhere else. This scene covers communication and the organisation of information only: the route and whether to divert are decided by the driver under traffic rules, navigation and the road conditions, and are not argued while driving; if it needs discussing, stop somewhere safe first, and handle any incident or breakdown under traffic police and recovery guidance.

Both hold the same information: fuel left, the detour time from navigation, where the others originally wanted to go, and the latest time to turn back. One more often puts "what does everyone want from this trip" first: who has looked forward to it for ages, whose expectation is disappointed by a change; the other more often puts "do the constraints hold for everyone equally" first: is there enough fuel and time, and do the things promised in the original plan still count.

Both reasons appear and both miss something: attending only to expectations may ignore the fuel gauge, attending only to constraints may leave the carful of people unhappy. Who answers which message first is not a criterion — who was driving and who was reading navigation decides that far more than type. Before the next trip, put both "where we most want to go" and "the latest time to turn back" into the group, and both questions get answered, which is more useful than watching who answers first.
sections.title: ESFP and ESTP at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
The first misread is giving each a label: risk-taking to ESTP, sociability to ESFP. Whether someone steps up in a sudden situation depends on experience, physical capacity, duty and how many people are present; both types can step up, and both can finish a stock count quietly.

The second is judging by spending and saving habits. Consumption style alone cannot separate T from F; a spending decision also has to be read against income, family responsibilities and the goal at the time, and those conditions usually bear more directly than preference.

The third slip is writing T as "only numbers, no humanity" and F as "only feelings, no rules". ESTP will also stand up for a colleague who has been treated badly, and ESFP can cut an unprofitable category by a rule. What can be compared is the reason: does it more often cite "can this standard be applied consistently", or "what does this mean for the people involved". Both reasons are used by both, a single phrasing is not a criterion, and it has to be read across comparable situations.
sections.title: ESFP and ESTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring convention first, then the situation you answered from: a recent job change, a new colleague to train, a target just assigned — such conditions amplify one side. None of it allows a stable tendency to be inferred from one score.

Put the practice on real decisions and record three things: what options and constraints there were, what you finally based the trade-off on, and what would change your mind. Take a few recent small matters about display, scheduling or purchasing, write a few lines for each, and look back once several are filled; that is more useful than trying to recall who you resemble during a test. If "is the standard consistent" or "what does it mean for people" keeps appearing, it is worth discussing as your judging habit; it is not a typing rule. When results disagree, check the item bank, the language and the answering situation, and do not treat behaviour when alone, or some fixed number of occasions, as the arbiter.
sections.title: ESFP and ESTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Both may adjust the colour scheme first, and both may move the position first; the difference is which reason is cited more often when deciding.

In front of the same information, one more often asks "what does this mean for people coming into the store, and should the promised display be honoured", the other more often asks "is this rule consistent across all categories". Both reasons are used by both; the order of adjusting colour and moving position depends on the role, the staffing and the footfall at the time, and cannot type anyone.
items.question: With the same display, what does each attend to?

items.answer:
Because a type is the whole arrangement of four positions, not only the first.

The two share Se dominant and Ni fourth; what separates them is the auxiliary, Fi against Ti, and the third, Te against Fe. That is emphasis inside the model and does not predict behavioural order or a field of expertise; the labelling of the third position is disputed across sources, so check whether a differing version states its convention.
items.question: They share the same dominant — why are they still two types?

items.answer:
Both do. Anyone can learn to assess how a display feels to customers and what it costs. Both are often part of the job.

Anyone managing a store for long watches the lighting angle and the margin sheet. What can be compared is not whether they can, but which reason is cited more often when deciding: whether the standard can be applied consistently, or what this means for the people involved. A single phrasing is not a criterion; read several situations together.
items.question: ESTP also cares about atmosphere, and ESFP also counts cost?

items.answer:
Both can do it; do not divide by type.

Display work means setting the banding rules, the positions and the materials, and who finds which part easier depends on the seasons they have worked, the data in hand and the staffing. A workable approach is for each to write a version and test both against the same season's sales, margin, shrinkage and footfall counts, then decide who owns which part. Type does not enter the evaluation sheet.
items.question: Who is better suited to display or promotion planning?

items.answer:
Often where the two cite different reasons and each hears the other rejecting them.

One says "this rule cannot be broken for a single item", the other says "we promised to keep it over there", and it sounds like rules against people. Write the two kinds of reason on the same sheet: which standards must hold, who is affected, what this season's goal is, then set the boundary. The boundary is decided by the task and the result, not by type.
items.question: Where might a pair of them get stuck?

items.answer:
Check whether both used the same questionnaire, language version and scoring convention; one score cannot decide.

Record each result, the scene you referred to (a project at work, a situation at home) and the items you hesitated over. If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at whether T/F sits near the boundary; a score near the dividing line means the T/F label may be sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two types both hold. Do not treat "what I do when nobody is watching" or a fixed number of occasions as the arbiter.
items.question: I have tested as each once — how do I judge which is steadier?

The preference definitions follow the [official Myers-Briggs facts page](https://www.myersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's account of type dynamics processes](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/). These sources support the description of preferences and type dynamics; they contain none of the behaviour, trading results or business advice in the scenes on this page.

The four-position arrangement used here (Se–Fi–Te–Ni for ESFP, Se–Ti–Fe–Ni for ESTP), especially the attitude of the third process, is the common writing adopted editorially; sources handle it differently, and this writing is not presented as the Foundation's only version.

The seasonal display, the mid-autumn set-up, the short-dated discount and the weekend drive are all editorial fictions, corresponding to no real store, person or event, used only to practise discrimination, and constituting no business, discount or driving advice; driving and safety judgements follow traffic law, on-site guidance and professional recovery advice.

Assessment results are not for ranking ability, screening candidates or predicting relationships; trading data is used only to check a plan, not to infer a type.

The FermatMind assessment uses its own item bank and scoring; the scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence note](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
